similarities.point: Both describe a buttress as a structure built against a wall to support it.
similarities.quote_britannica: BUTTRESS, a kind of batment built archwise, or a mals of flouse or birds, serving to prop of flapper the fides of a building, wall, 6e, on the outside
similarities.quote_wikipedia: A buttress is an architectural structure built against or projecting from a wall which serves to support or reinforce the wall.

similarities.point: Both mention that buttresses are used to support walls bearing heavy loads such as roofs.
similarities.quote_britannica: along the walls of such buildings at have great and heavy roofs, which would be subject to shrull the walls once, unless very thick, if no butteffes were placed against them.
similarities.quote_wikipedia: as a means of providing support to act against the lateral (sideways) forces arising out of inadequately braced roof structures.

differences.point: Britannica describes buttresses as being used against the angles of steeples and old palaces, while Wikipedia mentions ancient temples and classifies buttresses by ground plan.
differences.quote_britannica: Butteflies are used against the angles of fleeples and other buildings of slone, 6e, on the confiile, and along the walls of such buildings at have great and heavy roofs
differences.quote_wikipedia: Early examples of buttresses are found on the Eanna Temple (ancient Uruk), dating to as early as the 4th millennium BC.

differences.point: Britannica mentions buttresses supporting the feet of fine arches in old palaces and abbeys, while Wikipedia discusses types such as clasping, angled, setback, and diagonal buttresses.
differences.quote_britannica: They are also placed for a lupport and bammer against the feet of fine arches, that are turned around great halls in old palaces, abbys, cz.
differences.quote_wikipedia: A clasping or clamped buttress has an L-shaped ground plan surrounding the corner, an angled buttress has two buttresses meeting at the corner, a setback buttress is similar to an angled buttress but the buttresses are set back from the corner, and a diagonal (or 'French') buttress bisects the angle between the walls where they meet.
